solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Here, Brits' earliest of soap operas is broadcast

definitions.text: Here, Brits' earliest of soap operas is broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is scattered widely, so the letters of the fodder are spread into a new order

parts.note: the possessive apostrophe adds no letter, so the word is used as written

indicators.note: the earliest letters of the two words soap and operas are taken

explanation.surface: A claim that Britain's first-ever soap opera is broadcast from right here.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the anagram of HERE, BRITS, S and O gives the county where The Archers, the long-running BBC radio soap, is set.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional county in which the radio serial The Archers takes place is the 'here' of a very old British soap.

clue.text: Period on jetty ignoring the odd rowing team?

parts.note: October, a period of the year, is abbreviated OCT

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered letters of jetty keeps only its second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A spell waiting on a jetty for a rowing crew to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a group of eight in music also describes the eight oarsmen of a racing boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of eight, which is what a rowing eight is; hence the question mark as a definition by example.

clue.text: Boozer extremely brave to interrupt actor

indicators.note: one piece breaking into another, so the outer letters of brave go inside the actor's name

parts.note: Martin or Charlie Sheen, the American actors

indicators.note: the extreme letters, first and last, of the word brave

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker bravely heckles a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' looks like a drinker but is the British slang for a pub; a shebeen is an unlicensed drinking den, originally Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a boozer is a pub, and a shebeen is an illicit bar or drinking house.

clue.text: Whistleblower gives this ultimately — drop ball — in case of squabble

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the casing formed by the other

parts.note: a tiff is a minor squabble

indicators.note: the ultimate, final letter of the word drop

parts.note: a ball is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A referee blows his whistle after a dropped ball sparks an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistleblower' suggests a referee but is an informer, and the definition is the thing such a person gives.
explanation.definitionFit: An informer passes on a secret warning or piece of confidential information to the authorities.

clue.text: Mecca cash bingo latterly raised money prize

indicators.note: the latter, last letters of the words cash and bingo
in a down clue, raised means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the yen is Japanese money
a pot is the prize money to be won, as in a jackpot

explanation.surface: A Mecca bingo hall advertising its cash jackpot.
explanation.walkthrough: Mecca is a British chain of bingo halls, which colours the surface; the definition uses mecca as any place that attracts crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: A mecca is a place drawing many visitors, just as a sweet attraction draws bees and tourists.

clue.text: Chicken, not a sausage, served in roll

indicators.note: something served in a roll is placed inside it, as filling

parts.note: a roll is a list of names, a rota or roster
British slang for nothing at all, so zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A chicken roll with no sausage in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a sausage' is British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A cockerel is a male domestic fowl, so a kind of chicken.

clue.text: Masseur down in basement of building on guided tour?

parts.note: a masseur is someone who rubs, a rubber
to down a drink is to neck it, in British slang

indicators.note: in a down clue, the basement is the bottom letter of building

explanation.surface: A masseur working downstairs in a building's basement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like a direction but means to swallow quickly; 'neck' is British slang for that.
explanation.definitionFit: Gawping and craning the neck at sights is what tourists on a guided coach trip do, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Train-robber on part of roof whispered very much

indicators.note: whispered words are spoken softly, so the sound of the phrase gives the answer

parts.note: Ronnie Biggs of the Great Train Robbery, beside a tile, part of a roof

explanation.surface: A fugitive train robber hides up on a roof, murmuring.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie Biggs was a member of the 1963 Great Train Robbery gang in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial phrase means in a big way, to a great extent, just like a lot.

clue.text: Partner stops mongrel heartlessly breaking kitchen utensil

indicators.note: one piece stops up, plugs, the other, so it goes inside
breaking signals the letters are broken up and rearranged
without its heart, the central letter of the word mongrel

parts.note: a squeeze is a colloquial term for a boyfriend or girlfriend

explanation.surface: Someone's partner breaks up a fight with a stray dog in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' leaves MONREL, 'breaking' makes LEMONR, and 'stops' plugs the partner into it. 'Partner' as a lover is informal British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget for pressing juice out of citrus fruit is a standard piece of kitchen equipment.

clue.text: Striking tune embodies Minnelli's latest release

indicators.note: to embody is to take into the body, so one piece holds the other
striking can mean hitting or knocking about, so the letters are knocked into a new order
the latest, final letter of the name Minnelli

explanation.surface: A catchy tune features on Liza Minnelli's newest record release.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' rearranges TUNE to UNTE, and 'embodies' sets I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or bonds is to free or let go, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Cat I'm displaying in shop window perhaps: Puss in Boots?

indicators.note: goods displayed in a window sit inside it, so these pieces go inside

parts.note: a pane of glass, as in a shop window
a tom is a male cat
the letters of the word without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A cat sits displayed in a shop window, dressed as Puss in Boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: Puss in Boots is a fairy tale often staged as a British Christmas family show.
explanation.definitionFit: Puss in Boots is a traditional story staged as a festive theatrical show in Britain, an example of the genre.

clue.text: Stroke insect

definitions.meaning: a swimming stroke with both arms moving together over the water
a winged insect with large colourful wings

explanation.definitionFit: One word names both a swimming stroke and a brightly winged flying insect.

clue.text: Till conceals key chain

indicators.note: one piece conceals the other by holding it within

parts.note: till means up to, so the word to
Esc is the escape key on a keyboard

explanation.surface: A cash till hides the key on a chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Till' looks like a cash register but means until; the chain is the British supermarket group.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's largest supermarket business is a chain of stores across the country.

clue.text: Yorkshire division on horseback

definitions.meaning: historically Yorkshire was split into three administrative areas, North, East and West

explanation.definitionFit: The English county of Yorkshire was once split into three parts with this name, and the word also means travelling astride a horse.

clue.text: Stand in river to conduct flipping exercise

indicators.note: to conduct is to lead or carry, so one piece carries the other inside it

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland

indicators.note: flipped over, the word is read in reverse

parts.note: a sit-up is an abdominal exercise

explanation.surface: Someone stands in a river conducting a ridiculous exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns SITUP to PUTIS, and DEE carries it. 'Stand in' looks like where to stand, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To act as a substitute for someone is to step into their role temporarily.

clue.text: Person with bins agreed to follow warning about untidiness, initially

indicators.note: the word for agreed follows, coming after, the earlier pieces
the warning word goes around the next piece

parts.note: fore is the golfer's warning shout

indicators.note: the initial, first letter of the word untidiness

parts.note: yes signals agreement

explanation.surface: A neighbour agrees after a warning about the untidy dustbins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bins' looks like rubbish bins, but it is British slang for spectacles, from binoculars.
explanation.definitionFit: A taunting nickname for someone who wears spectacles, here called bins in slang.

clue.text: Deposit cash in dog-eared tens

indicators.note: the cash goes inside the rearranged letters
dog-eared pages are worn and bent out of shape, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: a dime is a coin, a bit of cash

explanation.surface: Someone banks money held in tatty old ten-pound notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog-eared' gives SENT, with the coin set 'in' it. 'Deposit' looks like a banking verb, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Matter that settles at the bottom of a liquid is a deposit, in the geological or chemical sense.

clue.text: English policeman during intercourse, falling back, bursts a blood vessel?

indicators.note: one piece occurs during, so inside, the other
falling back reads the word backwards

parts.note: sex is sexual intercourse
plod is British slang for a police officer, from PC Plod in the Noddy books

explanation.surface: An English officer caught in flagrante gets furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling back' gives XES, with the officer 'during' it. Bursting a blood vessel is an idiom for flying into a rage, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To burst a blood vessel is to erupt in fury, which is to go off with rage.

clue.text: Toppings of Luigi's Italian pizza dressed with mayo — or plain?

indicators.note: a salad is dressed by tossing, so the letters are tossed into a new order
the tops, first letters, of the words Luigi's, Italian and pizza

explanation.surface: Choosing pizza toppings at Luigi's: with mayonnaise or without?
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain' looks like an unadorned pizza, but it is a flat stretch of land in Greece, site of the ancient Games.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Games of Greece were held on a level valley in the Peloponnese, so it is an example of a plain.

clue.text: Roughly-speaking, are you familiar with overseas capital?

indicators.note: spoken roughly, slurred, so the sound only approximates the phrase

parts.note: to ask if someone is familiar with something is to ask do you know

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a listener knows a capital abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone is loose: 'do you know' said fast and slurred.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Alaska, a US state, is a seat of government across the ocean from Britain.

clue.text: Fellow extremists in nude, stirred, but not shaken

indicators.note: the first pieces go inside the rearranged letters
stirred, mixed up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the extreme letters of the alphabet, A and Z

explanation.surface: Fellow radicals, naked, stirred but not shaken like a Bond martini.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirred' gives UNED, with the fellow and extremists placed 'in' it. The surface plays on James Bond's martini, shaken not stirred.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unshaken is calm and unperturbed, not put out at all.

clue.text: Vincent museum here in central Europe

parts.note: Gene Vincent was an early rock'n'roll singer
the V and A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London

explanation.surface: A Van Gogh museum located somewhere in the middle of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vincent' suggests Van Gogh but supplies the singer's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss city on Lake Leman lies in the heart of the continent, so is a place there.

clue.text: Strip emptied tiny pool

parts.note: a strip is a sports team's kit

indicators.note: the word is emptied of its middle letters, leaving the outer two

explanation.surface: Someone strips out and drains a tiny swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' is a noun, a team's football outfit, and 'pool' is a fund rather than water.
explanation.definitionFit: A shared fund of money contributed by several people, as in a card game or office whip-round.

clue.text: Energy forces inhabit Blaine magic? It's beyond words

indicators.note: the first pieces live inside the rearranged letters
magic transforms, so the letters are changed into a new order

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy
F is the abbreviation for force, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: David Blaine's magic leaves viewers speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'magic' rearranges BLAINE into INABLE, with EFF set inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something too great to be expressed in speech is indescribable, so it is beyond what language can convey.

clue.text: Fish most common in babbling brook

parts.note: the letter appearing most often in the word babbling, three times
a rill is a small stream

explanation.surface: A fish that is plentiful in a burbling stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most common in babbling' asks which letter appears most often in that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatfish related to the turbot, found in European seas.

clue.text: Relative entertains foreign brass, retrieving some of glasses

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to take them in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a niece is a relative

indicators.note: retrieving is read as re-trieving, bringing back, so the word goes backwards

parts.note: brass is slang for money; the peso is a foreign currency

explanation.surface: A relative entertains foreign top brass and pours drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrieving' gives OSEP, which the relative 'entertains'. 'Glasses' suggests drinks, but here they are spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: The bridge of a pair of spectacles that rests on the nose is a component of them.

clue.text: Shelled Brazil nuts, heading for export somewhere abroad, recalled?

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order
shelled means the outer letters, the shell, of the word Brazil are removed
the heading, first letter, of the word export

explanation.surface: Shelled Brazil nuts headed for export, then recalled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' rearranges RAZI to ZAIR. 'recalled?' marks a country that is now only remembered, under an old name.
explanation.definitionFit: The former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a country now only remembered by that title.

clue.text: Max keeps painting beach with defects showing

indicators.note: one piece keeps, holds, the others inside

parts.note: Max Wall was a British comedian
a painting is a work of art
a beach is made of sand

explanation.surface: Max keeps a painting of a beach that shows its blemishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Wall was a British music-hall comedian, famous for his funny walk.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning with all faults included, nothing hidden, from Cromwell's instruction to his portrait painter.
